heading: CHAPTER XXIV.
title: WHY THE PRINCES OF ITALY HAVE LOST THEIR STATES
exclusions: front matter and dedication before THE PRINCE
notes: Chapter 24 turns the earlier advice into a diagnosis of failure. Princes lose states not because fate suddenly turned, but because they ignored the disciplines already laid down.

Machiavelli names three recurring failures: weakness in arms, hostility from the people, or failure to secure the nobles. Philip of Macedon functions as the counterexample showing that a ruler who keeps those supports can survive severe pressure.
The chapter ends by rejecting rescue fantasies. Neglected rulers flee, hope to be recalled, and blame fortune, but only defenses that depend on oneself and one's valour are reliable.
